title: Waitress the Musical | REVIEW
transcript: Hello, hello, you lovely lot, and welcome or welcome back to a brand new video here on my stagey YouTube channel. It's been a while, but today I'm back and I'm going to be sharing with you all of my thoughts and feelings about the brand new UK tour of Waitress the Musical, which just opened at the New Wimbledon Theatre. So, grab an apron, a big slice of pie, and let's get into this. If you're new here, let me catch you up real quick on how this is all going to work. My name's Laura, and I have a lot, and I mean a lot of opinions when it comes to all things theater. Am I qualified to have these opinions? Some might say no, but I like sharing them with the internet anyway. Typically, I split my reviews into the highlights and the lowlights. It's just easier for me to structure my thoughts that way, in a way that hopefully makes sense to you. And it's also important to point out that everything shared in this review is based in my opinion and my opinion alone. So, you are more than welcome to disagree with me. Also, a big thank you to the team over at the New Wimbledon Theatre, as well as Waitress the Musical, for having me along to check this show out to review for you guys. Now that that disclaimer is out of the way, let's get into this. Now, I'm going to bring you up to speed on all things Waitress the Musical before we get into actually talking about this brand new production. This UK tour of Waitress the Musical is a replica of the Diane Paulus-directed Broadway and West End runs previously, and it stars Katharine Hope Fletcher as Jenna. Alongside a female director, the bulk of this show's creative team were also women, which I absolutely love. This includes a book by Jessie Nelson, songs by Sara Bareilles, and choreography by Lorin Latarro. The musical is, of course, based on the 2007 movie of the same name, and it follows the story of Jenna. She is a waitress and a pie maker who, at the end of the day, just dreams for happiness in her life. But that life becomes a whole lot more complicated when she finds out she's pregnant, and the new doctor she goes to see is absolutely gorgeous. With the support of her workmates and friends Becky and Dawn, Jenna overcomes the challenges she's facing, and according to the official website, finds that laughter, love, and friendship provide the perfect recipe to true happiness. Now, it's also worth pointing out that this is the first ever production of Waitress I have ever seen. I've not seen any of the previous productions from the UK. I've not watched the musical movie, either, and I've never listened to the cast recording. So, I was going into this completely blind, save for the fact that I have a lot of friends who are very deeply attached to this musical. So, bearing in mind I had no idea what to expect going into this, just how did I find it? The first thing I have to highlight is, of course, the cast. Now, this show did have some returning Waitress alumni, including Sandra Marvin and Evelyn Hoskins as Becky and Dawn, respectively. And of course, for the bulk of this tour, it is going to be starring Katharine Hope Fletcher. And I really loved the casting for this show. As a general rule, I think the chemistry, particularly between Jenna, Dawn, and Becky, was spot on. It really did feel like they'd been working in this small pie shop forever, and therefore knew each other to the point where they had little in-jokes and were okay teasing each other. But at the end of the day, just had a deep love and friendship with one another. Katharine's voice as Jenna, I think, was beautiful. The way she sang "She Used to Be Mine", of course, one of the big hits from the show, was absolutely stunning. And I think because she is such a recent mother herself, she brought that energy to the role of Jenna, which was really lovely to see. I think just about all of the actors in this show played really well against one another, particularly Sandra and Dan, who play Becky and Cal. Their chemistry was really good. I liked the fun back-and-forth bickering old married couple energy they had going on. And everyone to a degree did feel quite believable as someone who had spent their whole lives in a small town in the south of America. Dan Partridge's Dr. Pomatter, as well, had a really fun golden retriever energy about him. I think the notes I scribbled down when I was actually watching the show said good-natured frat boy. There was something kind of overly confident, but bumbling and confused at the same time, which I think really helped endear the audience to him. I will say that, sadly, I don't think the chemistry between the characters of Jenna and Dr. Pomatter were quite where I expected it to be, given that their affair is such a driving force throughout the plot of the show. But at the same time, the show has literally only been open like four days, so it's understandable that that is chemistry that's going to continue to grow throughout the show as Katharine and Dan spend a lot more time in one another's company, playing off one another. Another really fun thing about this show was the decision to have the band on the stage at all times. But more specifically, the fact that the band was set up so it looked like they were part of the diner. They were all sat on similar chairs and bar stools to the patrons of the diner, which was really lovely. And the piano itself was being used as a sort of display for the various pies throughout the show, which I thought was a really natural and quite clever way to blend them in with the rest of the show, as opposed to just having them kind of like sit there not doing a whole lot aside from playing music. I really enjoy it when musicals choose to include the band on the stage, because I think it's quite easy for audiences to forget that the band is such a driving force, particularly in a musical, creating the ambiance, atmosphere, and music that is driving the songs through the story. They help sell the atmosphere, and so for this show to have them on stage so they can be given their dues almost throughout the show, as opposed to just kind of gestured to during the bows at the end, is really lovely. But I will say I do think this production fell short in more ways than I was definitely expecting going into this, given how much everyone had sung the praises of this musical and really talked it up to me prior to me going to see it. I think the first big disappointment or letdown or lowlight for this show for me was the set. Now, of course, I have no idea how similar this set was to what was on the West End or Broadway, but it felt very flat and bland. And completely understand there are quite strict limitations when it comes to touring a production around, as to how feasible it is to move large set pieces and kind of anything overly techy, overly complicated, that adds such an expense and so many logistical nightmares to a touring production that I understand maybe simplifying it and scaling it back. But at the same time, I was kind of looking at it being like, I have seen school productions with better sets than this. And I think this was a feeling really compounded by the kind of lack of lighting direction throughout the show. Quite often, everything just felt quite flat and quite bland and quite boringly lit, to be honest. There was no real depth or warmth at any moment. It felt quite cold. You know how they light movies now, where everything's lit quite flat so that they can add CGI in later? It felt like that. It felt very flat, and I think that was quite disappointing. A lot of the set outside of the diner, which is arguably the big set piece and the centerpiece for the musical, were just kind of like a painted wall with like black curtains hung around it. And I was kind of just left wanting a little bit more. Again, this is probably because the set has to be so adaptable to the various sizes of venues it's going to be touring through, but I just feel like we could have maybe been a bit more creative, particularly with how we were lighting such a simple set to create extra dimension and extra warmth throughout each scene. Another area that I found this show slightly confusing or lacking, perhaps, was the choreography. This show had quite a big ensemble, which I wasn't really expecting, but their entire purpose seemed to kind of be just to waft pies or baking ingredients around as a character sang like that, and I didn't really feel like they were adding anything. I totally understand that you can't really set a show in a diner without having patrons visiting the diner, and the ensemble was certainly there to fill that role in to a degree. But the choreography they were given often just felt quite redundant to the story it was being told. It didn't feel very well considered or artistic or, you know, adding to the visuals of what was being presented on stage. I feel like you could have removed them and still had whoever was singing on stage singing out, and very little would have changed about that. And for me, when choreography and things like that feel redundant, it kind of pulls me out of the story or out of the musical as I'm watching it, because I'm kind of going, "What are you guys ordering here?" Then a real point of contention, I want to say, for me with this show was the characters of Dawn and Ogie. Now, I don't know whether it was deliberate direction or not, but there was something about the way both the characters of Dawn and Ogie were played that didn't quite sit right with me. Both characters felt like they teetered very close to being portrayed as neurodivergent stereotypes, and that that specifically was being played for laughs for a good chunk of the time they were on stage. Character quirks, such as missing social cues, being particular about the order the ketchup and mustard are organized in, and having niche interests that the other characters in the show deem as weird, all played into this and ultimately contributed to both the characters being quite an uncomfortable watch. Now, of course, neither of them are explicitly stated to be any sort of neurodivergent, but as someone who is neurodivergent myself, when I see scenes like that, but as someone who's neurodivergent myself, when I see characters like that, I can't help but cringe, particularly when it is, like I say, being played for laughs. Ogie, too, was a character I really struggled with. He is the one who sings the song "Never Ever Getting Rid of Me". To me, it read very much more as a man who could not read the strong no that the woman in front of him was giving him, or the fact that he was making her uneasy, than it read as a romantic, if not comedic, expression of love. The scene before the song begins is Dawn realizing he's basically come and sat in the place that she works after their brief date the night before, and panicking because she doesn't know how she feels about him. She wasn't sure after their date. And to me, at least, it felt like she was leaning more towards no than she was leaning towards yes. But he changes her mind, basically saying, "You're never getting rid of me, no matter what you do." And in seeing this expression from Ogie, her friends go, "Well, Dawn, you're a bit weird. How many other guys are going to say they love you? You should just settle for him." It felt like Jenna and Becky very much had this like perspective that Dawn was a weird woman, and therefore, how many other guys are going to come along that will ever like a gal like her, and therefore, she should just get with Ogie, which I feel was just very poor handling of the situation being presented on stage, and poor decision-making from the characters that are supposed to be Dawn's friends. And I think this was made worse by the almost patronizing ahs coming from the audience throughout the scenes that they were together. Now, it does appear that by the end of the show, the two of them are very happy, they get married, and they have a kid. That is very much established throughout the show. So, it clearly works out, but I was just so uncomfortable watching both of their characters, particularly in this "You're Never Ever Getting Rid of Me" scene, because yes, while neither of them are explicitly stated to be any sort of neurodivergent, whether it was actor choice or direction, there was a lot of traits and actions that veered very much towards neurodivergent stereotypes, and it was just a bit uncomfy. And I just feel like it could have been handled a lot better. So, those are my highlights and my lowlights, the kind of official review, if you will. But I would also like to continue this by saying, kind of more personally, I just did not enjoy this musical. I know a lot of people have a very deep love for it. They talk about it being a musical that they found when they were younger, fell in love, saw it, and a lot of people that were there the night I went were telling me how this was like their sixth, seventh time seeing it. They adored it. They always listen to the music. And so, I went in expecting to really connect to it, really emote, feel something from it. And I just kind of sat there Bored's a bit of a harsh word, but I just felt so over it. I think I personally really struggled to connect with any of the characters, be it because of their decision-making or the way they were behaving and acting. And so, I think because I lacked that emotional connection to any of the characters, I wasn't really pulled along on this emotional journey. I can appreciate how others can feel something towards this show. I just don't think I am the target audience for it, certainly. Which is a shame because I went in wanting to love it, and it just didn't hit the nail on the head for me in the way I expected it to. Whilst this tour is part of the celebration of the 10th anniversary of this musical, I did actually leave the theater thinking, "Hang on a minute, I think I may have actually enjoyed this show more if it had been a non-replica production." Now, I appreciate that was never going to happen as, like I said, it was the 10th anniversary of this specific production of Waitress the Musical. But I do think perhaps if I went to see it again with different direction, different design, different choreography, and all of that, that I might actually be able to get into it and enjoy it a little bit more. But unfortunately, in its current form, Waitress the Musical is not a musical I can say I particularly care about. But there you go. Those are all of my thoughts and feelings on the brand new production of Waitress the Musical. I'm trying to keep these reviews short and sweet, not just for you so you can enjoy it in one short sitting, but also for myself so I don't have to spend 8 hours editing it. So, hopefully this slightly more condensed, shorter review is something that works for you. I know I may have upset quite a lot of Waitress fans. So, if you do disagree with me, let me know in the comments. I'd love to have a discussion about what you love so much about this musical. I know I have a couple of very exciting reviews coming up for you guys. So, make sure you're subscribed so you don't miss out on more amazing stagey content that will be coming your way in the near future. If you enjoyed this video, be sure to give it a thumbs up. And as always, guys, I'll see you in the next one. Bye.
